newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's national service plan questioned.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's national service plan questioned.

text.p: A key Malaysian youth group and an opposition leader have questioned the wisdom of proposed compulsory non-military national service for young people, local news reports said on Tuesday.
The Star newspaper quoted the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) youth education committee chairman as saying the government should focus on expanding existing activities.
"What is the point of imposing something new? What we should do is expand and develop what we already have," the Star quoted UMNO's Khalid Nordin as saying.
UMNO is the leading party in Malaysia's ruling National Front coalition.

On Monday, Deputy Education Minister Fong Chan Onn was quoted as saying a national service programme may be made mandatory for all Malaysian secondary school graduates as well as those pursuing tertiary courses.
The programme was proposed last week as one way to combat social problems among the country's Moslem population.
Fong said the programme would focus on good moral and civic values and include a "character-building plan" for youths leaving school, he said.
The Youth and Sports Ministry is working on a paper on national service. The non-military service could be modelled along the lines of summer camps in the United States.

Parliamentary opposition leader Lim Kit Siang, of the Democratic Action Party, said schools should focus on character-building before youths graduate, the national Bernama news agency reported on Tuesday.
"At most, compulsory national social service can only address the symptoms but not the root causes of social problems of youths," Lim said.
He suggested the Cabinet hold a national education conference to study the causes of social problems among the nation's youth.
Malaysia does not have military conscription, so the proposed scheme would be the country's first compulsory national service for young people.
It recently launched a campaign against drug abuse, incest and crime besetting the Moslem community, which make up more than half the country's 21 million people.
